body: Picture an old-fashioned set of kitchen scales, one pan on each side. Add a weight to one pan and the scales tip - unless you add the exact same weight to the other pan too. Take a weight off one side, and the other side has to lose the same amount to stay level.
An equation works the same way. The = sign says both sides are level right now. You're free to add, remove, or shift anything you like, as long as you do the identical thing to both sides at once.

teach.heading: Moving a term across the equals sign
body: An equation is a balance: whatever you do to one side, you do to the other. Moving a term across the = is really adding or subtracting it from both sides at once - and that flips its sign.

transferOut.prompt: Where else have you seen something moved from one side to keep things level, flipping from adding to subtracting (or back) on the way? It could be about money, time, anything. Describe your own example in a sentence or two.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. when I pay a friend back £5, it comes off what I owe them and gets added to what I've paid off so far...

body: Overnight, a fridge's temperature drops by 12°C in total, falling at a steady 3°C an hour with the door left open. To find how many hours the door was open, you divide the total drop by the hourly rate - both negative, because both describe the same direction of change. A negative divided by a negative comes out positive: 4 hours, which is the only sensible kind of answer a number of hours can be.

teach.heading: Dividing by a negative number
body: Once the unknown term is on its own, divide both sides by its coefficient - including the sign. A negative divided by a negative gives a positive answer, so don't drop the sign on the last step.

transferOut.prompt: Think of your own moment where two negatives - both describing the same kind of drop, debt, or backward movement - divided out to leave an ordinary positive number. Describe it in a sentence or two.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. a diver going down 2m every minute reaches −18m after 9 minutes: −18 ÷ −2 = 9...

body: Two friends live at opposite ends of a straight road and want to meet where neither walks further than the other. You would not guess — you would find the point exactly halfway between the two front doors.
A midpoint on a grid is that same idea, done once for how far across you are and once for how far up. Nothing more complicated is going on.

teach.heading: The midpoint is the average of each coordinate
body: To find the point halfway between two others, average the two x values, then average the two y values. Those two answers are the x and y of the midpoint.
Averaging means add the pair and halve it. Do the x pair and the y pair completely separately — they never mix.

transferOut.prompt: Where else do you find something exactly halfway between two values — splitting a bill, a halfway point on a journey, the middle of a temperature range? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. when my sister and I split the cost of a present, we each pay halfway between nothing and the full price...

body: A £40 game goes up by 15%. The shop does not throw away the £40 and start again — the new price is the old price plus a bit more, and the 'bit more' is what the percentage describes.
Getting this right depends on being clear about what the percentage is a percentage *of*. It is always of the original amount, not of the new one.

teach.heading: Find the increase, then add it on
body: A percentage increase has two steps. First work out the increase itself: that is the percentage of the ORIGINAL amount. Then add it to the original.
Finding the increase and stopping there is the commonest slip — that answer is how much it went up by, not what it costs now.

transferOut.prompt: Where have you seen an amount go up by a percentage rather than a fixed amount — a price rise, interest on savings, a tip? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. my bus fare went up by 5% rather than by a set number of pence, so the longer journeys went up more...

body: If six identical pens cost 90p, you can answer almost any question about pens the moment you know what one costs. Everything else is multiplying up from there.
This is the single most useful trick in proportion, and it is why it has a name: find the value of one unit first.

teach.heading: Find one, then scale up
body: Divide to find the value of a single item, then multiply by however many you actually want. Two steps, always the same two steps.
The temptation is to jump straight from one quantity to the other. Going via one keeps it reliable even when the numbers are awkward.

transferOut.prompt: Where do you work out the cost or size of one thing before scaling up — shopping, cooking, splitting something between people? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. working out the price per 100g to see which packet is actually better value...

body: A recipe for four people needs 200g of rice. Cooking for eight, nobody calculates from scratch — you double everything, because twice the people needs twice of each ingredient.
That is direct proportion: both quantities move together by the same multiplier.

teach.heading: Find the multiplier, then apply it to everything
body: When two quantities are in direct proportion, doubling one doubles the other. So find the number you multiplied by, then use that same number on the quantity you want.
The multiplier need not be a whole number — scaling a recipe for four up to six means multiplying by 1.5.
teach.exampleTitle: 4 cakes need 300g of flour. How much for 12 cakes?

transferOut.prompt: Where have you scaled a whole set of quantities up or down together — a recipe, a paint mix, a plan drawn to scale? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. doubling a pancake recipe meant doubling the flour, the milk and the eggs, all by the same amount...

transferIn.hook: Three of everything in the bag
body: A party bag holds a drink and two sweets. Handing out three bags means three drinks and six sweets — the three multiplies everything inside, not just the first thing you happened to think of.
A bracket in algebra is that bag. The number outside multiplies every single term inside it.

teach.heading: Multiply every term inside the bracket
body: The number outside a bracket multiplies each term inside, one at a time. Two terms inside means two multiplications.
Multiplying only the first term and leaving the rest untouched is the classic mistake, and it is worth checking for deliberately every time.

transferOut.prompt: Where have you multiplied up a whole set of things at once rather than one of them — packing bags, ordering for a group, scaling a plan? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. ordering five meal deals means five sandwiches AND five drinks AND five packets of crisps...

body: If a parcel is inside a box inside a bag, you take the bag off first. Order matters, and the outermost wrapping goes first.
An equation with a bracket is wrapped the same way. Deal with the bracket, and what is left is an ordinary equation you already know how to solve.

teach.heading: Expand first, then solve as usual
body: Expand the bracket to get rid of it, then solve the equation exactly as you would any other: get the letters on one side, the numbers on the other, then divide.
Trying to solve before expanding is where this goes wrong — the bracket keeps the terms locked together and they cannot be moved independently until it is gone.

transferOut.prompt: Where do you have to undo something in a particular order — getting dressed, following a recipe, taking apart something you built? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. you cannot take the wheel off before you have loosened the nuts, no matter how keen you are...

body: A puzzle tells you two numbers add to 20, and that one is 4 bigger than the other. Neither clue alone is enough. Together they pin both numbers down exactly.
Simultaneous equations are two clues about two unknowns, and the trick is combining them so one unknown disappears.

teach.heading: Add the equations to make a letter vanish
body: When one equation has +y and the other has −y, adding them together cancels y completely, leaving a simple equation in x alone.
Once you have x, put it back into either original equation to find y. The cancelling is the whole point — you are choosing the move that removes a letter.
teach.exampleTitle: Solve x + y = 12 and x − y = 4

transferOut.prompt: Where have two separate pieces of information together told you something neither could alone — a bill and a receipt, two witnesses, two measurements? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. knowing the total shopping bill and the price of one item let me work out what the rest cost...

transferIn.hook: A letter is a box waiting for a number
body: A recipe that says 'cook for n minutes per kilogram' is useless until you weigh the joint. The n is a space waiting to be filled in.
Letters in algebra work the same way. Substituting is just filling the space with the number you have been given.

teach.heading: Replace the letter, then work it out
body: Swap the letter for its value, then do the arithmetic. Remember that 4p means 4 × p — the multiplication sign is invisible but it is definitely there.
Writing the × in yourself before calculating stops the commonest error, which is adding the number to the letter's value instead of multiplying.

transferOut.prompt: Where have you filled a number into a rule that was written in general terms — a cooking time, a delivery charge, a phone tariff? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. the parking sign said £2 per hour, so for 3 hours I worked out 2 × 3...

body: A journey cost is often 'so much per mile, plus a fixed booking fee'. Two different numbers, doing two different jobs, in one calculation.
An expression with two letters is the same. Each letter gets its own value and neither borrows from the other.

teach.heading: Substitute each letter separately
body: Replace every letter with its own value, then work through the arithmetic in the usual order: multiplications first, then the additions and subtractions.
Keep the two letters apart. Swapping which value goes with which letter is easy to do and impossible to spot afterwards.
teach.exampleTitle: Work out 3a + 2b when a = 4 and b = 5

transferOut.prompt: Where does a total depend on two different quantities at once — a taxi fare, a phone bill, a shopping trip with two kinds of item? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. my phone bill is a monthly fee plus a charge for every gigabyte over the limit...

body: A half, 0.5 and 50% are the same quantity wearing different clothes. Which one you use is about convenience, not about the amount changing.
Being able to move between them freely is what lets you compare things that were written down in different ways.

teach.heading: Divide, then multiply by 100
body: A fraction is a division waiting to happen. Do the division to get a decimal, then multiply by 100 to turn that decimal into a percentage.
Stopping after the division is the usual slip: that answer is the decimal, and calling it a percentage makes it a hundred times too small.

transferOut.prompt: Where have you seen the same amount written as a fraction in one place and a percentage in another — a sale, a test score, a battery indicator? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. my phone showed 25% battery and I thought of it as a quarter left...

body: A freezer at −18°C is colder than one at −4°C, even though 18 is the bigger number. Once you are below zero, the bigger the digit, the further down you are.
A number line makes that obvious: −18 sits further left than −4, and left always means smaller.

teach.heading: Negatives run leftwards from zero
body: Numbers get smaller as you move left along a number line and bigger as you move right. Zero is the middle, and negatives continue leftwards past it.
Moving left means subtracting. That stays true whether you are at 7, at 0, or already at −3.

transferOut.prompt: Where have you seen numbers carry on below zero — temperature, a bank balance, a lift going to a basement? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. the car park lift goes down to level −2, which is two floors below the ground floor...

body: Owing £30 is a worse position than owing £5, but −30 is the smaller number. People trip over this constantly, and it is worth being clear about once.
Smaller means further left on the line, which for debts means owing more.

teach.heading: Further left is always smaller
body: To compare two negatives, picture where each sits on the line. Whichever is further left is smaller, no matter which digit looks bigger.
The instinct to compare the digits and ignore the minus sign is the mistake to watch for.

transferOut.prompt: Where does 'more' actually mean a smaller number — debts, temperatures, points deducted? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. a friend owes more than me, so their balance is the lower number even though they say the bigger one...

transferIn.hook: The same slice, described two ways
body: Half a pizza and four eighths of a pizza are the same amount of pizza. Nobody eating it would notice a difference — only the description changed.
Simplifying is choosing the tidiest description of an amount that has not changed.

teach.heading: Divide top and bottom by the same number
body: A fraction stays worth the same if you divide the numerator and denominator by the same number. Keep going until nothing divides both.
Dividing only one of them changes the amount, which is the error to avoid — whatever you do above the line you must do below it.

transferOut.prompt: Where do you describe the same amount in tidier terms — a recipe, a score, a measurement? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. saying I got half marks rather than 17 out of 34...

body: Paying two thirds of a £30 bill is not guesswork: work out a third, then take two of them. The fraction tells you exactly how to split it.
Finding a fraction of an amount is one division followed by one multiplication, in that order.

teach.heading: Divide by the bottom, multiply by the top
body: Divide the amount by the denominator to find one part, then multiply by the numerator to get however many parts you want.
Doing it the other way round works too, but dividing first usually keeps the numbers small enough to do in your head.

transferOut.prompt: Where have you taken a fraction of an amount — splitting a bill, a discount, sharing something out? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. three of us split a £24 taxi, so we each paid a third...

body: A shop sign saying 0.25 off would baffle everyone; 25% off is instantly clear. Same number, and the percentage is just the friendlier costume.
'Per cent' literally means 'per hundred', which is why the conversion is a multiplication by 100.

teach.heading: Multiply the decimal by 100
body: To turn a decimal into a percentage, multiply by 100. The digits do not change — the decimal point moves two places right.
Going the other way, from a percentage to a decimal, you divide by 100 and the point moves two places left.
exampleSteps: The point moves two places right

transferOut.prompt: Where have you seen the same amount as a decimal in one place and a percentage in another? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. my running app shows 0.8 of the route done, but the progress bar says 80%...

body: Asked how far it is to the next town you say 'about 40 miles', not 38.6. Rounding trades a little accuracy for a number people can actually hold in their heads.
The rule is simple, and it is always about which side of halfway you are on.

teach.heading: Look at the digit to the right
body: To round to the nearest ten, look at the units digit. Five or more rounds up; less than five rounds down. The digits to the right become zero.
The digit you are rounding TO is not the one you look at — you look at the one immediately after it.
exampleSteps: 7 is 5 or more, so round up

transferOut.prompt: Where do you round rather than give an exact figure — distances, times, prices, crowd sizes? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. I tell people the journey takes half an hour when it is really 26 minutes...

body: Tiling a 12cm by 18cm rectangle with identical square tiles and no cutting, the biggest square that works is 6cm. That is the highest common factor, doing a real job.
The HCF is the largest number that divides both, which is exactly what 'fits into both without a remainder' means.

teach.heading: Find the largest number dividing both
body: List what divides each number, or split both into prime factors, and take the largest they share.
Confusing it with the lowest common multiple is easy: the HCF is smaller than both numbers, the LCM is bigger than both.

transferOut.prompt: Where have you needed the biggest size that divides two things evenly — tiling, cutting, packing, sharing? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. cutting two ribbons of different lengths into equal pieces with none left over...

transferIn.hook: Two parts squash to one part orange
body: A squash bottle says 1 part squash to 4 parts water. It works the same in a cup or a jug — the ratio describes the relationship, not the amounts.
Simplifying a ratio finds the smallest whole numbers that describe the same relationship.

teach.heading: Divide every part by the same number
body: Divide all the parts of a ratio by their highest common factor. The relationship is unchanged; the numbers just get smaller.
Every part must be divided, not just some of them — dividing one side only changes the mix.

transferOut.prompt: Where have you seen a mix described as a ratio — squash, paint, cement, a recipe? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. the paint tin said mix three parts paint to one part water...

transferIn.hook: Numbers too big to write out
body: The distance to the sun is about 150,000,000 km. Writing that out invites a miscounted zero, and comparing two such numbers by eye is hopeless.
Standard form writes any number as one digit, a decimal part, and a power of ten — compact and easy to compare.

teach.heading: One digit, then a power of ten
body: Move the decimal point until exactly one non-zero digit sits in front of it, then count how many places it moved. That count is the power of ten.
The power counts the places the point moved, not the number of zeros — those only coincide for round numbers.

transferOut.prompt: Where have you met a number too big or small to write comfortably — distances, populations, file sizes? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. my phone said the file was 2.4 GB rather than writing out the bytes...

transferIn.hook: An exact answer beats a rounded one
body: √8 is 2.828427... and never stops. Writing 2√2 instead keeps the value exact, and exact answers stay correct however many steps come after them.
Simplifying a surd pulls out whatever square factor is hiding inside the root.

teach.heading: Take out the largest square factor
body: Split the number under the root into a square number times something else, then square-root the square part and leave the rest inside.
Use the LARGEST square factor. Using a smaller one is not wrong, it just leaves you simplifying again.

transferOut.prompt: Where is an exact answer worth more than a rounded one — money, measurements, anything you build on later? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. rounding early when splitting a bill left us 3p short at the end...

body: If someone cancels £5 you owed, you are £5 better off. Removing a negative leaves you higher up — subtracting a negative is adding.
It sounds like a trick until you have a picture for it, and cancelled debt is the picture.

teach.heading: Subtracting a negative moves you right
body: Two minus signs together become a plus: 7 − (−3) is 7 + 3. Taking away something that was pulling you down leaves you higher.
Careful with the other direction: 3 − 7 is genuinely negative, and there is nothing wrong with an answer below zero.

transferOut.prompt: Where has something being removed left you better off — a cancelled charge, a refund, a penalty overturned? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. the shop took the £4 delivery charge off, so my total went up by less than I expected...

body: 'Not unhelpful' means helpful. Two negatives in the same sentence undo each other, and multiplication behaves the same way.
One negative flips the sign; a second flips it back.

teach.heading: Same signs give a positive
body: Multiplying two numbers with the same sign gives a positive; different signs give a negative. That covers every case.
Count the minus signs: an even number of them gives a positive answer, an odd number gives a negative one.

transferOut.prompt: Where do two negatives cancel in ordinary language or in life? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. saying I'm 'not unhappy' with my result really means I'm quite pleased...

body: To open a locked door you turn the key the other way. Solving an equation is the same move: whatever was done to x, you undo it.
Multiplication is undone by division, and addition by subtraction. Nothing more is needed for a one-step equation.

teach.heading: Undo the operation on both sides
body: If x has been multiplied by a number, divide both sides by that number. Doing it to both sides keeps the equation balanced.
The commonest slip is doing the same operation again instead of the opposite one.

transferOut.prompt: Where do you undo a step to get back to where you started — retracing a route, reversing a transaction? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. to work out the original price after 20% off, I had to undo the discount rather than take another 20% off...

body: A parking sign reading '£2 per hour' is a rule with a gap in it. Stay three hours and you fill the gap with 3.
Substituting is filling that gap with the number you have been given, then doing the arithmetic.

teach.heading: Replace the letter, then calculate
body: Swap each letter for its value and work the answer out. Remember 3x means 3 × x — the multiplication sign is invisible but real.
Writing the × in before you calculate prevents the usual error, which is adding the number to x instead of multiplying.

transferOut.prompt: Where have you put your own number into a general rule — a fare, a cooking time, a phone tariff? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. the recipe said 20 minutes per kilo, and my chicken was 2kg...

body: Algebra drops the × sign because it looks too much like the letter x. So 3a means 3 × a, and it is doing exactly that even though nothing is written.
Once you know the sign is there, expressions stop looking like codes and start looking like calculations.

teach.heading: Numbers and letters written together are multiplied
body: Write the number first, then the letters: 3 × a × 2 × b tidies to 6ab. Multiply the numbers and let the letters sit alongside.
Writing 32ab by putting the digits next to each other is the error to avoid — the numbers must actually be multiplied.

transferOut.prompt: Where is something left out because everyone knows it is there — a sign, a unit, a step? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. the recipe just said '180', because everyone knows that means degrees...

body: Three apples and two oranges and another four apples comes to seven apples and two oranges. You cannot add apples to oranges, and there is no need to.
Like terms in algebra are the same idea: only terms with the same letter can be added together.

teach.heading: Only add terms with the same letter
body: Group the terms that share a letter and add their numbers. Terms with different letters stay separate.
Merging x and y terms into one is the common mistake — 3x + 2y is already as simple as it gets.
exampleSteps: The y term is on its own

transferOut.prompt: Where do you group like with like before counting — sorting shopping, tidying, counting change? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. counting up my coins by sorting them into piles of the same value first...

body: Expanding takes a bracket apart. Factorising is the same journey in reverse — spotting what both terms share and pulling it outside.
If you can expand, you can check your factorising instantly, which makes this one of the safest things in algebra.

teach.heading: Take the common factor outside
body: Find the largest number (and any letter) that divides every term, write it outside a bracket, and put what is left inside.
Check by expanding: multiply back out and you should land exactly where you started.

transferOut.prompt: Where do you pull out something shared rather than repeat it — a shared cost, a common ingredient? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. instead of listing the delivery fee on every line, the invoice charged it once at the bottom...

body: A pattern going 5, 8, 11, 14 is easy to continue one step at a time — but nobody wants to count to the hundredth term that way.
A rule for the nth term jumps straight there, and finding it is mostly about spotting the step size.

teach.heading: The common difference is the coefficient of n
body: Work out how much the sequence goes up by each time. That is the number in front of n. Then adjust so the first term comes out right.
Stopping at the difference is the usual slip: 3n alone gives 3, 6, 9, so if the sequence starts at 5 you still need + 2.
exampleSteps: It goes up by 3 each time, so start with 3n

transferOut.prompt: Where have you spotted a rule that lets you skip ahead rather than counting step by step? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. working out what a saving would be after a year rather than adding it up week by week...

body: A sign reading 'maximum 8 people' does not mean exactly eight — it means eight or fewer. Plenty of real answers are a range rather than a single value.
Inequalities describe those ranges, and they solve almost exactly like equations.

teach.heading: Solve like an equation, but watch the sign
body: Do the same things to both sides as you would with an equation. The inequality sign stays pointing the same way — unless you multiply or divide by a negative, which flips it.
Dividing by a positive never flips it. That is the case to be sure of before worrying about the exception.
exampleSteps: 4 is positive, so the sign stays

transferOut.prompt: Where is the answer a range rather than one number — a speed limit, an age restriction, a weight allowance? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. the hand luggage limit was 10kg, so anything up to that was fine...

body: Working out the area of a garden that is (x + 3) long and (x + 2) wide means four rectangles, not two. Every part of one side meets every part of the other.
Expanding two brackets is that grid of four multiplications, then tidying up.

teach.heading: Multiply every term by every term
body: Each term in the first bracket multiplies each term in the second: four products from two brackets of two terms. Then collect the like terms.
Multiplying only the firsts and only the lasts is the classic error — it loses the two middle terms that make the x coefficient.

transferOut.prompt: Where does every part of one thing have to meet every part of another — seating plans, fixtures, combinations? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. in our league every team plays every other team, so the fixtures multiply up fast...

body: A door opened flat against the wall and then swung shut sweeps half a full turn. Wherever it stops, the angle in front of it and the angle behind it always add to that half turn.
That is all 'angles on a straight line add to 180°' means, and it is one of the most useful facts in geometry.

teach.heading: Angles on a straight line add to 180°
body: A straight line is half a full turn. Any angles sitting along it must add up to 180°, so a missing one is found by subtracting from 180.
Reaching for 360° is the usual mistake — that is a complete turn, not a straight line.
teach.exampleTitle: One angle on a straight line is 115°
exampleSteps: Angles on a line add to 180°

transferOut.prompt: Where have you seen something turn through a half or a quarter turn — a door, a handle, a junction? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. the tap goes a quarter turn from off to full...

transferIn.hook: How many tiles cover the floor
body: A kitchen floor 5 tiles across and 3 tiles deep takes 15 tiles. You could count them, or you could multiply — and multiplying is why area works.
Area counts the squares that fit inside a shape; perimeter measures the distance round the edge. Different questions, easily confused.

teach.heading: Area is length times width
body: Multiply the two side lengths to get the number of unit squares that fit inside. The answer is in square units — cm², m² — because you multiplied two lengths.
Adding the sides gives the perimeter, not the area. If the answer should be in cm² and you added, something has gone wrong.

transferOut.prompt: Where have you worked out how much surface something covers — flooring, paint, turf, wrapping paper? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. working out how many packs of laminate we needed for the front room...

body: A taxi charging £3 plus £2 a mile has a rule, and that rule draws a straight line. Every point on it is a journey you could actually take.
Working out points from the rule is how a line gets onto the grid in the first place.

teach.heading: Put x in, get y out
body: Substitute a value for x into the rule and calculate y. That pair (x, y) is one point on the line. A few points and you can draw it.
Multiply before adding: in y = 2x + 3 with x = 4, it is 8 + 3, not 2 × 7.

transferOut.prompt: Where does a cost or amount follow a fixed rule with a starting figure plus a rate? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. my gym charges a joining fee plus a monthly amount...

body: Draw lines from one corner of any polygon to all the others and it falls into triangles. A pentagon gives three; a hexagon gives four — always two fewer than the number of sides.
Since every triangle's angles add to 180°, that immediately gives the angle sum of any polygon.

teach.heading: Angle sum is (n − 2) × 180°
body: Split the shape into triangles from one corner. An n-sided polygon gives n − 2 of them, each contributing 180°.
Multiplying by n instead of n − 2 is the usual slip — a quadrilateral gives two triangles, not four.

transferOut.prompt: Where have you broken an awkward shape into simpler ones to measure it? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. working out the carpet for an L-shaped room by treating it as two rectangles...

body: A box 4 cubes long, 3 wide and 2 high holds 24 cubes. Multiply the three dimensions and you have counted them without stacking a thing.
Volume is that count — how much space is inside.

teach.heading: Volume is length × width × height
body: Multiply all three dimensions. The answer is in cubic units — cm³, m³ — because three lengths were multiplied.
Multiplying only two gives an area, not a volume. Check the units: cm² means something has been missed.

transferOut.prompt: Where have you worked out how much fits inside something — a box, a tank, a suitcase, a fridge? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. checking whether the new fridge would actually hold a week's shopping...

body: Pushing a book across a table moves it without spinning it. Every corner travels the same distance in the same direction, and the book stays the same size and the same way up.
A translation is exactly that slide, described by how far across and how far up.

teach.heading: Add the translation to each coordinate
body: A translation moves every point by the same amount. Add the horizontal shift to x and the vertical shift to y.
Negative shifts move left or down — the arithmetic is identical, so no special case is needed.

transferOut.prompt: Where does something move without turning or resizing — furniture, a piece on a board, a window on a screen? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. dragging an app icon to a different spot on the home screen...

transferIn.hook: The short cut across the park
body: Walking 30m along one path and 40m along another at right angles takes 70m. Cutting straight across the grass is only 50m — and Pythagoras is what tells you so without pacing it out.
The diagonal of a right-angled triangle is always shorter than going round the two sides, and always longer than either one.

teach.heading: a² + b² = c²
body: Square both short sides, add them, then square-root the total. That gives the hypotenuse — the side opposite the right angle, always the longest.
Adding the sides without squaring is the error to watch for: 30 + 40 is 70, but the answer is 50.

transferOut.prompt: Where have you cut a corner diagonally rather than going round two sides? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. the worn path across the field where everyone cuts the corner...

transferIn.hook: Rolling a wheel one full turn
body: A bike wheel rolled through exactly one revolution covers its own circumference. Do that with any wheel and the distance is always a bit over three times the width across.
That 'bit over three' is π, and it is the same for every circle that has ever existed.

teach.heading: Circumference = 2πr
body: Multiply the radius by 2 to get the diameter, then by π. Leaving π in the answer keeps it exact.
Confusing it with the area formula πr² is the usual trip — circumference is a distance, so the radius appears once, not squared.
teach.exampleTitle: Circumference of a circle with radius 7cm

transferOut.prompt: Where does something roll or wrap around a circle — a wheel, a tin label, a running track? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. working out how much ribbon would go round a round cake...

body: Counting cars going past, people use gate-five tallies rather than trying to remember a running number. The marks do the remembering.
The frequency is just how many marks each row ended up with, and the total is all of them added together.

teach.heading: Add every frequency for the total
body: Each row's frequency is its count. Add every row to get how many things were recorded altogether.
The number of categories is not the total — five rows can easily hold fifty items between them.

transferOut.prompt: Where have you kept a tally rather than a running total — a game, stock, a survey, a headcount? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. marking off each round on a beer mat so nobody argued about whose turn it was...

body: Three people bring 4, 6 and 8 sweets and pool them. Shared equally that is 6 each — the mean is what everyone would get if it were levelled out.
That is why you add everything then divide: you are pooling, then sharing.

teach.heading: Add them up, divide by how many
body: Add every value, then divide by how many values there were. The answer sits somewhere between the smallest and the largest.
Dividing by the wrong count is the usual error. Count the values, not the categories or the largest number.

transferOut.prompt: Where have you levelled something out to a fair share — splitting a bill, an average score, miles per week? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. working out what we each owed after one person paid for everything...

transferIn.hook: How spread out, not how big
body: Two classes can average the same test score while one is tightly bunched and the other has everything from 20 to 95. The average hides that completely.
The range is the simplest measure of how spread out a set of values is.

teach.heading: Largest minus smallest
body: Find the biggest value and the smallest, and subtract. That single number says how far the data stretches.
The range is a difference, not a value from the list — so it is usually smaller than any of the numbers you started with.

transferOut.prompt: Where does the spread matter more than the average — delivery times, temperatures, exam results, journey times? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. my commute averages 30 minutes but ranges from 20 to 55, so I always leave early...

transferIn.hook: Counting the ways it can go right
body: A bag with 3 red and 5 blue counters holds 8 counters. Three of the eight are red, so pulling one out blind, the chance of red is 3 out of 8.
Probability is that comparison: how many outcomes you want, against how many there are altogether.

teach.heading: Wanted outcomes over total outcomes
body: Count the outcomes you want, count all the outcomes, and write the first over the second. Simplify if it will.
Comparing red to blue instead of red to the total is the classic error — the bottom of the fraction is always everything.

transferOut.prompt: Where have you judged a chance by counting how many ways something could happen? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. two of the ten raffle tickets left were mine, so I fancied my odds...

body: Plot revision hours against test scores for a class and the dots scatter, but they trend upwards. A line through the middle lets you estimate a score for hours nobody actually did.
That line is the pattern, drawn through the noise.

teach.heading: Use the line, not the dots
body: Once a line of best fit is drawn, estimate by reading off it: put your x value into its rule and get y.
Estimating far outside the data is where this stops being reliable — the pattern is only evidenced where the dots are.
teach.exampleTitle: Line y = 4x + 10, estimate y when x = 6

transferOut.prompt: Where have you predicted something from a trend rather than an exact figure — growth, weather, revision, savings? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. guessing what my next electricity bill would be from the last few...

body: The chance of rain is 3 in 10 and the chance your bus is late is 2 in 10. The chance of both, on an independent day, is much smaller than either — bad luck twice over is rarer than bad luck once.
Multiplying along the branches of a tree diagram is how that gets calculated.

teach.heading: Multiply along the branches
body: For independent events, multiply the probabilities to get the chance of both. Multiply the tops together and the bottoms together.
Adding them is the usual error, and it gives an answer bigger than either — which cannot be right for 'both happening'.

transferOut.prompt: Where did two things both have to go right — a connection to catch, two results to go your way? Describe your own example.
transferOut.placeholder: e.g. I needed my train to be on time AND a seat free to get any work done...
